race_context: The 'Grant Mississinewa Community School Board' races on the state list are for the Mississinewa Community School Corporation, based in Gas City in Grant County {in_list}{mcsc_vacancy_packet}. The district says it serves Gas City and Jonesboro and runs four schools: Westview Elementary, Northview Elementary, R.J. Baskett Middle School and Mississinewa High School {mcsc_district}. Its per-school figures (about 450, 700, 600 and 750 students) add up to roughly 2,500 students {mcsc_district}. The district accepted 597 out-of-district transfer students in 2025-26, down from 700 the year before {ct_enroll_2025}.
The superintendent is Jeremy Fewell, who started on July 1, 2024 {ct_contract_2026}. On March 16, 2026, the board voted 7-0 to extend his contract through June 30, 2029 {ct_contract_2026}.

The board has seven members. One is elected from each of Districts 1, 2 and 3, and four are elected at large in District 4 {ct_2022_results}{ct_2024_results}{ct_transport_2026}. Terms are four years {mcsc_vacancy_packet}. Denny Smith is board president and Chris Cunningham is vice president {ct_2025_officers}{ct_transport_2026}. In 2026 the other members are Jarrett Richards, Kyle Speakman, Mike Crouch, Conrad Herrera and Lani Stearns {ct_transport_2026}{ct_staffing_2026}{mcsc_portal}.
District 2 (one seat): Conrad Herrera won the seat in 2022 and is running unopposed {ct_2022_results}{ct_ballot_2026}.

District 3 (one seat): Michael D. Crouch was re-elected without opposition in 2022 {ct_2022_preview}{ct_2022_results}. He is not on the 2026 ballot, so the seat is open. Robert Couse is the only candidate {ct_ballot_2026}{in_list}.

District 4 at large: two seats, not one. The state list says 'vote for 1' {in_list}, but the Chronicle-Tribune lists the race as 'District 4 At Large (vote for 2)' {ct_ballot_2026}{ct_contested_2026}. Denny Smith and Susan Miller won the two at-large seats on the 2022 ballot {ct_2022_results}. Miller resigned in 2026 after moving out of the district {ct_vacancy_2026}. In April 2026 the board appointed Lani Stearns to serve through Dec. 31, 2026, and the seat was put on the November ballot for a term from 2027 through 2030 {mcsc_vacancy_packet}{ct_fills_2026}. Smith and Stearns are both running, and Zach Aument (American Solidarity) is challenging them {ct_contested_2026}{in_list}.

Budget and the 2025 property-tax law (fall 2025): in October 2025 the district said its operations fund 'will be completely depleted by the end of 2026' because of circuit-breaker losses and Senate Enrolled Act 1 (SEA 1) {ct_opsfund_2025}. Its forecast showed the fund going from a $1.39 million positive balance in 2025 to a $1.13 million deficit in 2027 {ct_opsfund_2025}. In February 2026 the district said SEA 1 'is projected to reduce Mississinewa's Operations Fund revenue by an additional $1.2 million annually by 2028' {ct_transport_2026}.

Building plans (October 2025): the district dropped plans for a capital (building) referendum and turned to an operating referendum instead {ct_capital_2025}{mcsc_referendum}. Fewell said this 'doesn't make the issues at R.J. Baskett go away' {ct_capital_2025}.

Transportation (December 2025 - February 2026): the board heard public comment in December 2025 on a proposal to end bus service {ct_fight_2025}. The district says transportation costs about $1.2 million a year {ct_fight_2025}. The board put off its Jan. 12 vote until all members could attend {ct_tabled_2026}. On Feb. 16, 2026, it voted 5-0 to end the transportation program in 2027-28 if voters reject an operating referendum in November 2026 {ct_transport_2026}. The district says it would still have to transport students with an IEP {ct_transport_2026}.

Operating referendum (Nov. 3, 2026 ballot): on June 15, 2026, the board voted 7-0 to place an operating referendum on the ballot {ct_referendum_2026}. The question asks for up to $0.4950 per $100 of assessed value for no more than eight years, capped at $2 million a year, to pay for 'student transportation, school security upgrades, and the competitive compensation needed to recruit and retain teachers and staff' {ct_ballotq_2026}. Under the question, the tax bill on a $150,000 median home would rise by $294 a year {ct_ballotq_2026}. Fewell said ending transportation 'would be catastrophic for the district' and could lead to consolidation 'five to 10 years out' {ct_referendum_2026}.

Staffing (spring 2026): the district carried out a reduction in force and plans to cut central-office staffing from five positions to two between summer 2026 and summer 2027, the Chronicle-Tribune reported {ct_reshuffle_2026}.

2027 budget (September 2026): the board held its public hearing on the 2027 budget, capital projects plan and bus replacement plan on Sept. 21, 2026. The same agenda included a bond lease hearing and resolutions on a lease and construction bids {mcsc_agenda_20260921}.

Forums: this guide found no 2026 candidate forum or questionnaire for these races. In 2022 and 2024 the Chronicle-Tribune printed candidate answers or short profiles {ct_2022_qa}{ct_2024_preview}. The only contested race is the District 4 at-large race, with three candidates for two seats {ct_contested_2026}.

candidates.summary: Incumbent, running unopposed for another term in District 2 {ct_2022_results}{ct_ballot_2026}.
background: In a 2022 Chronicle-Tribune questionnaire he said he grew up in the community, attended Mississinewa schools and is 'a proud Mississinewa alum' {ct_2022_qa}.
Was elected board secretary in January 2025 {ct_2025_officers}.
path_to_ballot: Ran as the incumbent in 2022 and won the three-way District 2 race with 1,013 votes (45.65 percent) {ct_2022_preview}{ct_2022_results}.
Filed for reelection; The Indiana Citizen's copy of the state list gives May 19, 2026 as his filing date {incitizen_list}. The state lists him as Nonpartisan {in_list}.

items: In 2022 he said the community's vision is 'education, safety of the students and faculty' and that he would 'continue to support the education, safety of our students and faculty' {ct_2022_qa}.
In 2022 he promised to 'continue to have open lines of communication between myself and the community I represent' {ct_2022_qa}.

on_incumbent: In 2022 he described the board's role as overseeing and voting 'on policies, personnel and financials' and selecting and supporting the superintendent {ct_2022_qa}.

On April 20, 2026, he seconded the motion to appoint Lani Stearns to the vacant at-large seat. The motion passed unanimously {ct_fills_2026}. On July 27, 2026, he moved to approve the year's personnel changes, which passed 7-0 {ct_staffing_2026}.
gaps: No 2026 interview, questionnaire or campaign website was found.

No statement from him on SEA 1, the transportation resolution or the 2026 operating referendum was found; news reports did not record his individual vote on the June 15 referendum resolution beyond the 7-0 total.
Occupation not found in sources read.
No campaign finance reports were found.

candidates.summary: The only candidate for the open District 3 seat; incumbent Mike Crouch is not on the ballot {ct_ballot_2026}{ct_2022_results}.
path_to_ballot: Filed for the seat; The Indiana Citizen's copy of the state list gives June 18, 2026 as his filing date {incitizen_list}. The state lists him as Nonpartisan {in_list}.
gaps: No news coverage, candidate statement, website or social media page was found for this candidate.
Occupation, community roles and ties to the schools are unknown.
No campaign finance reports were found.

candidates.summary: Incumbent and board president, seeking another at-large term; voters choose two of three candidates {ct_2025_officers}{ct_contested_2026}.
background: Was elected board president in January 2025 as the only nominee {ct_2025_officers}. He was still president in February 2026 {ct_transport_2026}.
path_to_ballot: Won an at-large seat in 2022 with 1,384 votes (50.62 percent of votes in the two-seat race) {ct_2022_preview}{ct_2022_results}.
Filed for reelection; The Indiana Citizen's copy of the state list gives May 19, 2026 as his filing date {incitizen_list}. The state lists him as Nonpartisan {in_list}.

items: Before the Feb. 16, 2026 vote on the transportation resolution, he said, 'Just to reiterate, we are not canceling transportation today,' and added, 'We're just fulfilling our legal obligation.' {ct_transport_2026}

on_incumbent: After the April 2026 appointment of Lani Stearns, he said: 'We've been lucky, we've had good candidates, really good board members and a good strong support.' {ct_fills_2026}
gaps: No 2026 interview, questionnaire or campaign website was found.
Occupation and background not found in sources read.
He was absent from the Jan. 12, 2026 meeting, which led the board to postpone the transportation vote (Chronicle-Tribune, Jan. 13, 2026); no other attendance record was reviewed.
No campaign finance reports were found.

candidates.summary: Incumbent by appointment: the board named her in April 2026 to fill the rest of Susan Miller's at-large term, and she is running for a full term {ct_fills_2026}{ct_contested_2026}.
path_to_ballot: Ran for an at-large seat in 2024 and finished third of four candidates with 1,300 votes (22.84 percent); two seats were filled {ct_2024_results}{ct_2024_reelected}.
Appointed by the board on April 20, 2026 after public interviews of three applicants {ct_fills_2026}.
Filed for the seat; The Indiana Citizen's copy of the state list gives June 16, 2026 as her filing date {incitizen_list}. The state lists her as Nonpartisan {in_list}.

items: In 2024 the Chronicle-Tribune wrote that she 'aims to be a positive voice for students and educators, focusing on building relationships and maintaining open communication' {ct_2024_preview}.

on_incumbent: On July 27, 2026, she seconded the motion to accept $11,250 in donations, which the board approved unanimously {ct_staffing_2026}.
gaps: No 2026 interview, questionnaire or campaign website was found.
Occupation and community roles not found in sources read.
No statement from her on SEA 1, transportation or the operating referendum was found.
No campaign finance reports were found.

candidates.summary: A high school teacher from Gas City running as the American Solidarity Party candidate for one of two at-large seats {asp_aument}{ct_contested_2026}.
background: According to the American Solidarity Party, he lives in Gas City and 'currently teaches high school economics, finance, and government' {asp_aument}.

The party's profile says he spent 'nearly twenty years in pastoral and nonprofit leadership' and was 'a former consultant for the Indiana Department of Education and the Governor's Workforce Cabinet' {asp_aument}.
path_to_ballot: Filed with an American Solidarity Party affiliation; The Indiana Citizen's copy of the state list gives June 3, 2026 as his filing date {incitizen_list}{in_list}.
The American Solidarity Party lists him among its current candidates {asp_aument}.

items: His party profile says 'students deserve both deep academics and solid career pathways—whether leading to university classrooms or skilled trades' {asp_aument}.
The profile says he is committed to 'supporting parental rights, lesson transparency, and frontline teachers' {asp_aument}.
The profile says he would steward 'community resources with integrity' {asp_aument}.

endorsements_finance: Listed as a candidate by the American Solidarity Party {asp_aument}.
gaps: The party profile does not say which school he teaches at; whether he teaches in the Mississinewa district was not confirmed.
His campaign Facebook page could not be read without logging in.
No statement from him on SEA 1, the transportation resolution or the operating referendum was found.
No news coverage or forum answers were found; no campaign finance reports were found.
